Inductor andTorch-TensorRT speedups are computed from local synced benchmark_results.json files; FACT speedups are taken from the corresponding local pattern-table benchmark artifacts. For GEMMs, eager is PyTorch+cuBLAS with TF32 enabled (allow_tf32=True). This figure is intentionally separate from the pattern-ablation figure to keep compiler-backend effects distinct from pattern-composition effects.

Figure 6: KernelBench 44_MiniGPTBlock on A100 with (𝐵,𝑇 ,𝐶) = (128, 512, 768). (a) End-to-end latency for PyTorch baseline, single-pattern optimizations, and both patterns composed. (b) Speedup relative to the PyTorch baseline measured in the same benchmark run as each optimized configuration (ablations leave the non-target subgraph in eager PyTorch).

Figure 1: Pattern mapping hierarchy. The agent identifies optimization patterns from the computation graph, each associated with a rule (e.g., GEMM, FMHA). The pattern table T indexes kernels by a tuple (𝑟, 𝜏, 𝛼) capturing rule, data type, and target architecture, enabling retrieval of workloadmatched CUTLASS implementations.

Figure 2: Three-stage agentic workflow for whole-model kernel optimization. Stage 1 (Pattern Discovery) extracts and analyzes the computation graph to identify optimization opportunities. Stage 2 (Pattern Realization) synthesizes CUTLASS kernels for each pattern, verifying correctness and benchmarking performance before adding to the dynamic pattern table. Stage 3 (Pattern Composition) assembles the optimized kernels into a deployable model with PyTorch extensions and measures end-to-end speedup. LLM-based actions enable systematic execution of complex optimization tasks across all stages.
Figure 4: Auto-tuning results for all three Level 1 problems on A100. Each point is one configuration; stars mark the best. Dashed lines indicate parity with PyTorch (cuBLAS, TF32).

Table 2: Performance summary for all three Level 1 problems on A100. Throughput in TFLOPS. The PyTorch baseline uses cuBLAS with TF32 tensor cores enabled (allow_tf32=True). Default configurations are those used during initial verification; auto-tuned configurations are selected by exhaustive search over tile shapes and pipeline stages. The Scheduling column indicates the grid-level policy chosen by the agent at the Grid Level of the CUTLASS synthesis hierarchy.

Table 1: CUTLASS examples organized by KernelBench difficulty level and GPU architecture. Level 1: single linear algebra operators; Level 2: fused operators with epilogue or data movement fusion; Level 3: complex multi-operator patterns requiring interdependent scheduling decisions.

Figure 3: Three-level hierarchy of CUTLASS kernel synthesis. From innermost to outermost: (1) Tile-level primitives configure Tensor Core operations; (2) Kernel-level pipelining determines how memory-copy and compute overlap—warpspecialized designs onHopper versusmultistage pipelines on Ampere; (3) Grid-level scheduling controls work distribution across thread blocks. Each level presents distinct configuration decisions that the agent must resolve correctly for the target architecture and workload.
